name: Bullet Chart
summary: Tufte's replacement for the dashboard gauge: one measure, a target tick, and qualitative bands, in the height of a line of text. No script, no canvas, and a real table behind it.

attempts.prompt: Build a bullet chart component showing a value against a target.
attempts.problem: Produced a progress bar with a marker on it. The measure filled the full height of the track, which makes it read as a stacked bar rather than a measure sitting inside its context, and the target was a circle floating on top instead of a tick crossing the track. The qualitative bands were three separate divs laid side by side, so their widths were segment lengths rather than cumulative thresholds — the moment a threshold moved, every other width had to be recalculated by hand.

attempts.prompt: Fix the bands and make the measure thinner.
attempts.problem: Bands became cumulative but were still opaque colours stacked in DOM order, so the widest one painted over the others. Reversing the order fixed the paint but left the markup ordered backwards from how anyone would read it. Accessibility was untouched: a screen reader got three empty divs and a number, with no way to know what the bands meant or what the target was.

finalPrompt:
Build a bullet chart in plain HTML and CSS with no JavaScript, no canvas and no SVG.

The form matters precisely. A bullet chart is a measure bar sitting inside qualitative bands, with a target marked as a tick crossing the track. Three proportions carry that meaning: the bands fill the full height of the track, the measure is roughly a third of that height and vertically centred inside them, and the target is a two-pixel rule spanning nearly the full height. If the measure fills the track it reads as a stacked bar and the chart stops working.

Drive everything from four custom properties on the track element — --poor, --ok, --good, --value and --target — expressed as percentages. Bands are cumulative thresholds, not segment widths, so each band is positioned at left 0 with its own width and they are layered in reverse with z-index: the poorest band paints on top of the wider ones beneath it. Keep the markup in reading order and let z-index do the stacking. Moving one threshold must not require recalculating any other value.

Bands are tints of the foreground mixed into the background, so they read as context rather than as three coloured categories. Use the accent only to mark a measure that has beaten its target, via a data attribute on the measure.

Numbers are tabular-nums and right-aligned, with the unit in a smaller, lighter span so the digits align across rows.

A chart is a picture of a table, so ship the table: include a visually hidden table with a caption, column headers and row headers carrying the same figures, and give each row's track a role="img" with an aria-label stating the actual value, the target, and whether it is ahead or behind. Do not try to make the bars themselves readable to assistive technology.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--bg), var(--accent), with color-mix for the band tints. No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
The lesson here is about specifying form rather than naming a chart type. "Bullet chart" is well documented, and the model still produced a progress bar with a dot, because that is what most things called bullet charts on the web actually are. Naming the three proportions — bands full height, measure a third and centred, target a rule not a dot — is what produced the real form, and those three sentences did more than the name did.

The cumulative-versus-segment distinction is the kind of thing that looks like an implementation detail and is actually the whole maintainability of the component. Stating it as a property the result must hold — moving one threshold must not require recalculating another — got the layered z-index solution without my having to describe it.

And the accessibility instruction worked because it said what not to attempt. Trying to make bars themselves readable produces a pile of aria-label noise; saying a chart is a picture of a table, so ship the table, gets a real table and one honest summary per row.
